disease_info: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is characterized by one or more episodes of at least two weeks of pervasive low mood and/or loss of interest, accompanied by cognitive, physical, and emotional changes that cause significant distress or functional impairment. Core diagnostic features include changes in sleep, appetite or weight, energy, concentration, psychomotor activity, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, and recurrent thoughts of death or suicide, in the absence of a history of manic or hypomanic episodes. The course can be single‑episode or recurrent, with episodes often triggered or exacerbated by psychosocial stressors, medical illnesses, or substance use, but sometimes arising without an obvious precipitant. It is distinguished from grief, adjustment disorders, and bipolar depression by the persistence, pervasiveness, associated neurovegetative changes, and lack of mood elevation or distinct trigger‑linked pattern seen in other conditions.

narrative.personality: Latrina is a meticulous, disciplined, and quietly inquisitive woman who takes pride in organizing information, nurturing others, and preserving community history.
narrative.stressor: Over the past several months, Latrina has been dealing with worsening osteoarthritis and new-onset hypertension, leading to increased medical appointments and a physician advising her to cut back on standing, gardening, and long hours at the computer. She reluctantly scaled down her work on the Dayton civil-rights digital archive and stopped attending the community garden as frequently, which left her feeling as though the roles that had defined her retirement—organizer, mentor, and historian—were slipping away. As she spent more time at home alone, she began second-guessing her decisions and found it harder to plan her research or quilting projects, which frustrated her given her lifelong identity as someone precise and mentally sharp. After nearly a month of feeling unable to "get her mind to work right" enough to manage her archive tasks or mentor budgeting classes, she agreed to see her doctor when a fellow volunteer noticed she had abandoned several projects mid-way and seemed unusually hesitant and withdrawn.
narrative.chief_complaint: My mind just doesn’t seem to work the way it used to, and I can’t seem to focus or make decisions about even simple things.

narrative.personality: Paula is an outgoing, creative, and high-energy multitasker who thrives on social interaction, artistic expression, and spontaneous problem-solving.
narrative.stressor: Paula’s warehouse recently went through a restructuring, adding new productivity quotas and a stricter supervisor who dismissed her informal process-improvement ideas and wrote her up for minor mistakes. At the same time, a community arts grant she had pinned her hopes on for transitioning into an arts coordinator role fell through, leaving her feeling stuck in what she increasingly saw as a dead-end job. Over several weeks, she noticed that tasks she used to juggle effortlessly at work and in her creative life felt overwhelming to sort out, and she started avoiding decisions about shifts, bills, and even simple social plans, which was uncharacteristic for her normally decisive, improvisational style. When she missed an important inventory deadline and then found herself staring at a blank page for days instead of writing poetry or sketching, her choir director and a close friend urged her to seek help, leading her to schedule a mental health evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: I can’t seem to think straight or make up my mind about anything lately, even simple stuff I used to handle without thinking.

narrative.personality: Jessicca is a highly organized, analytically minded professional who prefers structured routines, solitary creative pursuits, and intellectual problem-solving.
narrative.stressor: Six weeks ago, Jessicca’s younger brother died unexpectedly in a car accident, an event that deeply shook her sense of control and safety, which had always been central to her work in security and risk assessment. She initially coped by throwing herself into long surveillance shifts and late-night forum reading, trying to distract herself with data and procedures, but found that the quiet hours only amplified intrusive reflections about his death and what she might have done differently in their relationship. As the weeks passed, her usual logical framework for understanding risk and probability offered little comfort, and her thoughts increasingly drifted toward the fragility of life and whether her own efforts and routines had any real meaning, making it harder to concentrate at work or engage with her art and hiking plans. After she confided to her spouse that she had been preoccupied with thoughts about not wanting to be alive and had started contemplating specific scenarios in which her absence might be a "relief" to others, her spouse insisted she see a psychiatrist urgently.
narrative.chief_complaint: Since my brother died, I keep thinking a lot about death and sometimes about not wanting to be here anymore.
